items.title: How to read an ECG
items.intro: A visual, repeatable system for anaesthesia and ICU, mapped to the ANZCA Final learning outcomes on ECG interpretation, life-threatening arrhythmias, conduction disease and ischaemia.

chapters.title: The 90-second routine
chapters.body:
> **THE RULE** Do not start by naming a diagnosis. First ask: Is the patient unstable? Then read the tracing in the same order every time. The ECG is a measurement of electrical activity, not a substitute for the clinical examination.

| **STEP** | **QUESTION TO ANSWER** | **WHAT TO SAY OUT LOUD** |
|---|---|---|
| 0 · SAFETY | Does this need action now? | Unstable rhythm, acute occlusion, severe K+ toxicity, high-grade block, marked QT prolongation? |
| 1 · VALIDITY | Right patient, calibration, artefact? | 25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV, compare an old ECG. Repeat poor-quality leads. |
| 2 · RATE | Fast, normal or slow? | R–R spacing / 300 rule, or count a 10-second strip ×6. |
| 3 · RHYTHM | Regular? Are P waves present? | Sinus? AF/flutter? AV relationship? Narrow or broad tachycardia? |
| 4 · AXIS + QRS | Frontal axis; width and shape? | Lead I/aVF. BBB, ventricular rhythm, pre-excitation or paced QRS? |
| 5 · INTERVALS | PR, QRS, QTc? | Conduction disease, long-QT/torsades risk, toxicity. |
| 6 · ST–T + Q | Regional ischaemia? Changes by territory? | Contiguous leads + reciprocal changes; posterior/RV views when needed. |
| 7 · SYNTHESISE | What matters for this operation? | One-line interpretation + immediate action or further investigation. |

> **THE FOUR PATTERNS TO NEVER MISS** Broad-complex tachycardia (presume VT if uncertain); unstable bradycardia / high-grade AV block. Acute coronary occlusion pattern, including posterior infarction or subtle STEMI equivalents. Hyperkalaemia or other drug/electrolyte toxicity causing QRS widening or malignant arrhythmia. Marked QTc prolongation with ventricular ectopy / torsades risk; pre-excited AF is another dangerous broad, irregular rhythm.

Exam mapping: ANZCA Final BT_PO 1.1 (ECG abnormalities and perioperative management), IT_PO 2.3 (interpret investigations), IT_PO 1.7 (life-threatening arrhythmias), IT_PO 1.4 (conduction disease / pacemakers) and the myocardial-ischaemia components of cardiac learning outcomes.

chapters.title: 1. Understand what you are looking at
chapters.body:
![Original annotated schematic: one electrical beat. Vertical scale = voltage; horizontal scale = time.](lib-ecg-01.png)

## The grid and normal measurements

| **Measurement** | **Remember** | **Why it matters** |
|---|---|---|
| Paper speed | Usually 25 mm/s: small square = 0.04 s; large = 0.20 s. | Use this before calculating rate or intervals. |
| Voltage | At 10 mm/mV, 10 small vertical squares = 1 mV. | Beware half gain / low voltage / artefact. |
| P wave | Atrial depolarisation; sinus P usually upright in II, negative in aVR. | Identify sinus, atrial rhythm, AV dissociation. |
| PR | 120–200 ms (3–5 small squares). | Long = AV delay; short + delta = pre-excitation possible. |
| QRS | Narrow <120 ms. | ≥120 ms: BBB, ventricular/paced or pre-excited activation, toxicity. |
| QTc | Interpret with HR, sex, drugs, electrolytes; ≥500 ms is an important warning. | Torsades risk; not simply a “long T wave”. |

## Rate: learn just two methods

Regular rhythm: 300 ÷ number of large squares between consecutive R waves. Remember 300 · 150 · 100 · 75 · 60 · 50 (one to six large squares). Irregular rhythm: count QRS complexes on a 10-second ECG and multiply by six; if the printout shows a shorter strip, adjust for its true duration.

![Schematic: regular sinus rhythm. First confirm a P before every QRS, with a stable PR.](lib-ecg-02.png)

> **The first useful sentence** “At standard calibration, the rhythm is regular at approximately 75/min, with sinus P waves, a normal PR interval and narrow QRS complexes.”

chapters.title: 2. Lead geography and axis
chapters.body:
Each lead sees the same cardiac electrical vector from a different direction. Territorial changes are more meaningful than a single abnormal-looking waveform. Consider adjacent (contiguous) leads, reciprocal changes, and compare prior ECGs.

![](lib-ecg-03.png)

![Territory memory map (simplified): LAD most often anterior; RCA or circumflex often inferior; circumflex may cause posterior patterns.](lib-ecg-04.png)

## Axis in under ten seconds

![](lib-ecg-05.png)

Look at the net QRS in lead I, then aVF. Both positive → usually normal axis. I positive/aVF negative → check lead II: if II positive, mild leftward axis may still be normal; if II negative, left axis deviation (roughly beyond –30°). I negative/aVF positive → right axis deviation. Both negative → extreme axis. Always interpret with QRS morphology and clinical context.

> **A practical trap** New right axis deviation is not diagnostic of pulmonary embolism. Left axis with RBBB can mean bifascicular conduction disease. Lead reversal, dextrocardia, misplaced V1/V2 or artefact may produce misleading findings.

chapters.title: 3. Rhythm first: narrow versus broad
chapters.body:
> **The rhythm decision tree** REGULAR vs IRREGULAR → QRS NARROW vs BROAD → P WAVES and relationship to QRS → is the patient unstable? A very fast regular rhythm around 150/min is atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction until reasonably excluded. A broad tachycardia is VT until proven otherwise.

## Regular narrow: sinus tachycardia, AVNRT/AVRT, atrial flutter

![Schematic: regular narrow tachycardia; absent or retrograde P waves. Surface ECG alone often cannot distinguish AVNRT from orthodromic AVRT.](lib-ecg-06.png)

Sinus tachycardia usually has identifiable normal P waves and a physiological trigger (pain, hypovolaemia, sepsis, hypoxia, PE). In abrupt-onset regular narrow tachycardia, think AVNRT/AVRT; flutter may hide one flutter wave in each QRS at ventricular rate around 150/min.

![Schematic: sawtooth atrial activity at about 300/min with 2:1 ventricular conduction at about 150/min.](lib-ecg-07.png)

## Irregular narrow: most often AF

![Schematic: irregularly irregular QRS spacing, no consistent P waves and fine fibrillatory baseline.](lib-ecg-08.png)

AF can be triggered by postoperative inflammation, sepsis, hypoxia, electrolyte abnormalities, catecholamines or chronic valve/atrial disease. Assess haemodynamic compromise and underlying trigger before simply aiming for rate control. Unstable tachyarrhythmia caused by the rhythm → immediate synchronised cardioversion; stable cases need individual rate/rhythm and anticoagulation decisions.

## Broad tachycardia: treat uncertainty as VT

![Schematic: regular monomorphic broad-complex tachycardia. Assume VT in a structurally abnormal heart unless compelling contrary evidence.](lib-ecg-09.png)

Clues favouring VT: AV dissociation, capture/fusion beats, extreme axis, very broad QRS, concordance, previous MI or cardiomyopathy. No single sign rules it in or out. Assess pulse and perfusion before medications: pulseless VT/VF → defibrillation + ALS; unstable VT with a pulse → synchronised cardioversion (unless polymorphic/unsynchronisable, when defibrillation may be needed).

> **Do not give “SVT medications” to an uncertain broad rhythm** Especially avoid verapamil/diltiazem for undifferentiated broad-complex tachycardia. Irregular, very fast, variable-width QRS complexes should raise pre-excited AF; AV nodal blockers (including adenosine, digoxin, beta blockers, verapamil/diltiazem and IV amiodarone) may be dangerous. Seek immediate expert help.

chapters.title: 4. Bradycardia and AV block: count the P waves
chapters.body:
A slow rate alone is not a diagnosis: trained athletes may be well at 40/min. Look for perfusion, ischaemia, hypotension, HF, and high-risk conduction patterns. If P waves are hard to see, examine II and V1 carefully and use calipers or paper to march them through the tracing.

![Schematic: Mobitz I — progressive PR prolongation followed by a non-conducted P wave, then the cycle resets.](lib-ecg-10.png)

![Schematic: Mobitz II — stable conducted PR intervals with unexpected non-conducted P waves (not merely a pause from sinus arrest).](lib-ecg-11.png)

![Schematic: complete AV block — P waves march independently from a slower escape QRS. AV dissociation alone has other causes, so check the full context.](lib-ecg-12.png)

| **Pattern** | **Signature** | **Perioperative implication** |
|---|---|---|
| 1st-degree AV block | Every P conducted, PR >200 ms | Usually surveillance rather than an emergency. |
| Mobitz I | PR lengthens → dropped QRS | Often nodal/vagal; context and symptoms determine action. |
| Mobitz II | Non-conducted P with unchanged conducted PR | Infranodal disease likely: risk of progression; urgent senior review and pacing plan. |
| Complete AV block | P and QRS independent; atrial rate > escape | Immediate assessment of perfusion and temporary pacing readiness. |
| 2:1 AV block | Every second P non-conducted | Cannot confidently call Mobitz I vs II from the ratio alone. |

For unstable bradycardia, follow current ANZCOR 11.9/local ALS algorithm: treat reversible causes, consider atropine (500–600 micrograms IV repeated as indicated up to 3 mg), adrenaline/isoprenaline as appropriate and transcutaneous pacing as a bridge to transvenous pacing. Atropine may fail in infranodal block and is unsuitable in a denervated transplanted heart.

chapters.title: 5. QRS morphology, BBB, pacing and QT
chapters.body:
![](lib-ecg-13.png)
> RBBB pattern (V1): terminal R′; check broad S in I/V6.
![](lib-ecg-14.png)
> LBBB pattern (V6): broad/notched R; V1 usually negative.

| **Finding** | **How to recognise** | **Why it matters** |
|---|---|---|
| RBBB | QRS ≥120 ms; rsR′/dominant terminal R′ V1; wide terminal S I/V6. | May be chronic, PE/RV strain, ischaemia or conduction disease. |
| LBBB | QRS ≥120 ms; broad often notched R I/V5/V6; deep predominantly negative V1. | Masks ordinary ST analysis: use clinical context and Sgarbossa principles. |
| WPW in sinus | PR <120 ms, delta-wave upstroke, wide QRS. | Pre-excited AF can degenerate to VF if AV nodal blockers are given. |
| Ventricular pacing | Spike may precede QRS; broad LBBB-like ventricular morphology. | Check capture and sensing; new malfunction requires a device/pacing plan. |
| Long QTc | Measure from onset QRS to end T; correct for rate. QTc ≥500 ms is high risk. | Avoid QT-prolonging drug combinations; check K/Mg/Ca and treat pause-dependent torsades promptly. |

![Schematic: prolonged repolarisation. A long-looking QT needs formal measurement and rate correction, not eyeballing alone.](lib-ecg-15.png)

Use an ECG with a clearly defined T-wave end (often II or V5). QTc depends on correction method; Bazett may exaggerate QTc in tachycardia and under-correct in bradycardia. If substantially abnormal, repeat and manually confirm before treatment decisions.

> **ECG tells you about conduction, not necessarily the cause** Before an operation, a new LBBB, Mobitz II, complete block, long QTc or arrhythmia may change investigation, electrolytes, pacing readiness, drug selection, monitoring and postoperative destination. Compare with earlier ECGs.

chapters.title: 6. Ischaemia: identify the territory, not a single ST spike
chapters.body:
Read ST segments relative to a consistent baseline. Seek a pattern in contiguous leads, reciprocal changes and dynamic evolution. An ECG can show acute coronary occlusion without traditional ST-elevation thresholds; clinical concern should override a reassuring single recording.

![Schematic 12-lead: inferior ST elevation in II, III, aVF, with reciprocal depression in I/aVL. Not patient data.](lib-ecg-16.png)

Inferior territory: II, III, aVF. Consider right-sided leads V3R/V4R when hypotension with an inferior infarction suggests RV involvement. With RV infarction, avoid reflex nitrates or excessive diuresis when preload-dependent; manage haemodynamics and arrange urgent reperfusion review.

![Schematic 12-lead: anterior ST elevation in V2–V4 with additional lateral changes. Think LAD territory. Not patient data.](lib-ecg-17.png)

Anterior territory: commonly V2–V4 and possibly V1/V5/V6, I/aVL. New acute changes with chest pain, shock, pulmonary oedema or arrhythmia require urgent ACS evaluation, not observation until the troponin rises.

chapters.title: 7. The acute coronary occlusion patterns that hide in plain sight
chapters.body:
![Schematic: horizontal ST depression in V1–V3 can be the mirror-image of posterior ST elevation. Request V7–V9. Not patient data.](lib-ecg-18.png)

| **Pattern** | **Look for** | **Implication** |
|---|---|---|
| Posterior occlusion | ST depression V1–V3, tall R/upright T; confirm V7–V9. | Can be an occlusion MI without ordinary anterior ST elevation. |
| De Winter pattern | Upsloping ST depression at J-point + tall symmetric T in precordial leads. | Potential proximal LAD occlusion; immediate expert review. |
| Wellens pattern | Biphasic or deeply inverted T waves V2–V3, often pain-free after angina. | Critical LAD risk; do not exercise-stress test before cardiology assessment. |
| Diffuse ST depression + aVR STE | Global subendocardial ischaemia pattern. | May signal critical multivessel/left-main disease OR profound supply–demand mismatch; not specific for left-main occlusion. |
| LBBB/paced ischaemia | Concordant STE, concordant V1–V3 STD or excessive discordance. | Use modified Sgarbossa + context; do not treat every new LBBB as STEMI. |
| Pericarditis mimic | Widespread often concave STE + PR depression (aVR opposite). | Clinical context and echo matter; regional reciprocal changes favour occlusion, but neither criterion is absolute. |

> **ST elevation thresholds ≠ permission to ignore symptoms** Conventional thresholds: at least 1 mm in 2 contiguous leads except V2–V3, where sex/age thresholds differ (women ≥1.5 mm; men ≥40 y ≥2 mm; men <40 y ≥2.5 mm). Absence of these cut-offs does NOT exclude acute occlusion. Obtain serial ECGs, additional leads, bedside echo and urgent consultation if ongoing concern.

chapters.title: 8. Electrolyte and drug patterns in theatre/ICU
chapters.body:
![Schematic: tall narrow-based peaked T waves and broadening QRS. Severe hyperkalaemia may look very different — or nearly normal.](lib-ecg-19.png)

![Schematic: T-wave flattening, ST depression and prominent U waves (may create apparent long QT/QU).](lib-ecg-20.png)

| **Problem** | **Possible ECG changes** | **Anaesthetic action** |
|---|---|---|
| Hyperkalaemia | Tall peaked T, reduced/absent P, prolonged PR, broad QRS, brady/blocks, sine wave. | Assess urgency and blood gas/K; if ECG toxicity or severe suspected hyperK, stabilise membrane with IV calcium and treat K per local protocol without waiting for confirmatory ECG. |
| Hypokalaemia / low Mg | T flattening, ST depression, U waves, prolonged QU and ectopy. | Correct K/Mg and review diuretics/antiarrhythmics; heightened torsades risk. |
| Hypocalcaemia / hypercalcaemia | Hypocalcaemia → QT prolongation; hypercalcaemia → shortening. | Correct cause; interpret calcium with albumin/ionised Ca and clinical features. |
| Na-channel blocker toxicity | Broad QRS, terminal R in aVR, arrhythmias (e.g. TCA, flecainide). | Early senior toxicology help; targeted sodium bicarbonate for appropriate sodium-channel blockade. |
| QT-prolonging drugs | Long QTc ± pause-dependent polymorphic VT. | Correct electrolytes, review antiemetics/antibiotics/antiarrhythmics and avoid stacking risks. |

> **Hyperkalaemia trap** Serum K+ and ECG severity correlate poorly. A normal-looking ECG cannot rule out dangerous hyperkalaemia. Treat the clinical scenario, not just the T-wave shape.

chapters.title: 9. What changes your anaesthetic plan?
chapters.body:
| **ECG finding before/in theatre** | **Ask next** | **Practical consequence** |
|---|---|---|
| New AF / flutter | Unstable? Trigger? Duration? Anticoagulation? LV function? | Control physiology; decide rate/rhythm intervention and appropriate monitored destination. |
| Mobitz II / complete block | Syncope, escape rate, recent MI, medications, K? | Pacing capability and cardiology support; do not proceed casually with elective surgery. |
| New ST–T change or acute QRS pattern | Symptoms, BP, troponin/serial ECG, echo, old ECG? | Assess ACS vs supply–demand injury; stabilise, discuss delay/urgent cath-lab if indicated. |
| QTc markedly prolonged | Drugs, bradycardia, electrolytes, family history? | Avoid provoking torsades; correct electrolytes, monitor and prepare defibrillation. |
| BBB or paced tracing | Old vs new? Associated syncope/structural disease? | ST analysis may be unreliable; device plan if CIED; targeted assessment. |
| Peaked T/broad QRS with renal failure | Blood gas/K, medications, renal status? | Immediate hyperkalaemia treatment if clinically suspected and dangerous. |
| RV strain pattern | PE, pulmonary hypertension, RV failure? | Assess echo/clinical probability; avoid RV insults (hypoxia, acidosis, excessive airway pressures). |

## The answer template to say in a viva

> **EXAM SCRIPT** “This is a [regular/irregular] rhythm at approximately [rate], with [sinus/non-sinus] atrial activity. The QRS is [narrow/broad] with [axis and conduction findings], the PR/QTc is [normal/abnormal], and there are [territorial ST–T changes]. Overall this suggests [diagnosis/differential]. The immediate concern is [instability/ischaemia/arrhythmic risk], so I would [action], while checking [reversible factors/other tests].”

chapters.title: 10. Practice: name the pattern before reading the answer
chapters.body:
Work through these in the same order every time: rate → rhythm → QRS → interval → ST/T → clinical consequence. The images are original teaching schematics (not patient ECGs), deliberately simplified to help pattern recognition. Compare with real 12-lead examples linked at the end.

## CASE 1

An otherwise stable adult has postoperative palpitations. What rhythm is most likely? What information determines urgency?

![](lib-ecg-08.png)

Your one-line interpretation: ______________________________________________________________

## CASE 2

A patient after major surgery has a very regular tachycardia near 150/min. What diagnosis must you actively look for?

![](lib-ecg-07.png)

Your one-line interpretation: ______________________________________________________________

## CASE 3

A patient with previous myocardial infarction becomes hypotensive with a broad regular tachycardia. Immediate priority?

![](lib-ecg-09.png)

Your one-line interpretation: ______________________________________________________________

## CASE 4

An elderly patient has syncope with a ventricular rate around 35/min; P waves outnumber QRS complexes.

![](lib-ecg-12.png)

Your one-line interpretation: ______________________________________________________________

## CASE 5

Renal failure, missed dialysis, new bradycardia and a broadening QRS. What cannot wait for a lab result?

![](lib-ecg-19.png)

Your one-line interpretation: ______________________________________________________________

## CASE 6

An asymptomatic patient is taking several QT-prolonging drugs; ECG appears to have a long QT interval.

![](lib-ecg-15.png)

Your one-line interpretation: ______________________________________________________________

## CASE 7

Inferior ST elevation with reciprocal high-lateral depression in a hypotensive patient. What territory and additional leads?

![](lib-ecg-16.png)

Your one-line interpretation: ______________________________________________________________

## CASE 8

Chest discomfort with precordial ST depression V1–V3 rather than obvious ST elevation. What might be missed?

![](lib-ecg-18.png)

Your one-line interpretation: ______________________________________________________________

chapters.title: 11. Worked answers — compare your reasoning
chapters.body:
## CASE 1 · Atrial fibrillation

Irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm without organised P waves. Assess hypotension, chest pain, HF, altered consciousness; identify triggers including sepsis, hypoxia and K/Mg issues. If unstable because of AF, synchronised cardioversion; if stable, individual rate/rhythm and anticoagulation plan.

## CASE 2 · Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction

Classical atrial activity ≈300/min produces ventricular ≈150/min; flutter waves can be hidden. Check inferior leads/V1 or slow AV conduction under supervised care. Physiological trigger, anticoagulation and instability matter.

## CASE 3 · VT until proven otherwise

Regular broad-complex tachycardia with structural disease and shock strongly favours VT. Check pulse. If unstable with pulse, immediate synchronised cardioversion; pulseless → defibrillation/ALS. Do not delay for a perfect ECG taxonomy.

## CASE 4 · Complete AV block

P waves march independently through a slow escape rhythm; risk of asystole and low output. Obtain senior/cardiology help, correct reversible causes, arrange immediate temporary pacing capability, and treat unstable bradycardia per ANZCOR.

## CASE 5 · Severe hyperkalaemic toxicity

Peaked T waves, P-wave loss and broad QRS are red flags, but sensitivity is poor. Treat suspected severe hyperkalaemia with urgent monitored IV calcium and potassium-lowering therapies per local protocol while sending a blood gas and addressing the cause.

## CASE 6 · Prolonged QTc

Measure QT accurately in II/V5 and calculate QTc (prefer appropriate correction when HR markedly abnormal). Review drugs, K/Mg/Ca, bradycardia and congenital risk. QTc ≥500 ms and ectopy are particularly concerning. Avoid aggravating factors.

## CASE 7 · Inferior acute coronary occlusion

Contiguous STE in II, III, aVF with reciprocal depression I/aVL. Suspect RCA or circumflex territory; in hypotension assess for RV involvement, obtain V4R/right-sided leads and urgent reperfusion review. Avoid excessive preload reduction if RV infarction.

## CASE 8 · Posterior coronary occlusion pattern

Anterior ST depression V1–V3 may represent reciprocal changes of a posterior infarction (often LCx/RCA). Look for tall R/upright T in those leads, record posterior V7–V9, and discuss immediate reperfusion if acute occlusion is likely.

chapters.title: 12. Keep it consolidated: a five-minute weekly routine
chapters.body:
**1.** Day 1: print the first-page algorithm. Read three 12-lead ECGs (including one normal) in the exact sequence; say the interpretation aloud.

**2.** Days 2–7: do two ECGs per day from LITFL Top 150; write one diagnosis, one differential and one anaesthetic consequence before opening the solution.

**3.** Week 2 onwards: once a week, read five mixed ECGs. Keep an error log: which step did you skip (axis? P–QRS relationship? reciprocal change?)

**4.** After a gap: revisit only your error log and the high-risk chart. Pattern recognition improves with spaced active retrieval, not repeated passive rereading.

chapters.title: Key studies and practice-changing evidence
chapters.body:
**S1 · REVERT trial (2015).** Modified Valsalva improved conversion of haemodynamically stable regular SVT compared with standard manoeuvre; not for unstable tachycardia or undifferentiated broad-complex rhythm. [Original publication](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26314489/)

**S2 · Smith-modified Sgarbossa diagnostic study (2012).** Proportional discordant ST elevation improves recognition of coronary occlusion in LBBB; diagnostic study, not a treatment RCT. [Original publication](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22939607/)

chapters.title: Linked references and genuine ECG examples
chapters.body:
**ANZCA Anaesthesia Training Program Curriculum v1.14** — Final Examination perioperative investigations, conduction disease, arrhythmias and ischaemia learning outcomes. [Open source](https://www.anzca.edu.au/education-and-training/anaesthesia-training-program/anaesthesia-training-program-curriculum)

**LITFL ECG Library** — Best freely accessible genuine clinical ECG examples, guided cases and ECG basics. [Open source](https://litfl.com/ecg-library/)

**ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 (2026)** — Australasian acute dysrhythmias, cardioversion, bradycardia/pacing, AV nodal-blocker cautions. [Open source](https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias)

**National Heart Foundation of Australia/CSANZ ACS guideline (2025 guideline, published 2026)** — Occlusion MI including STEMI equivalents, posterior and RV infarction, serial ECG/urgent action. [Open source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12907536/)

**Fifth Universal Definition of MI (2026)** — New diagnostic framing, ST criteria, hyperacute/de Winter/Wellens patterns, electrocardiographic limitations. [Open source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13523810/)

**Kim, Lever & Cooper: BJA Education (2023), part 1** — Arrhythmogenesis and perioperative risk factors. [Open source](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.11.001)

**Kim, Lever & Cooper: BJA Education (2023), part 2** — Perioperative antiarrhythmic drug principles and rhythm management. [Open source](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9845544/)

**AHA/ACC 2024 perioperative cardiovascular guideline** — Which preoperative ECG abnormalities warrant evaluation and when ECG testing is helpful. [Open source](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001285)

**2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS AF guideline** — Pre-excited AF, dangers of AV nodal blockade and arrhythmia assessment. [Open source](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2023.08.017)

**ECG gallery: atrial fibrillation (LITFL)** — Compare the schematic on page with real 12-lead tracings. [Open source](https://litfl.com/atrial-fibrillation-ecg-library/)

**ECG gallery: complete heart block (LITFL)** — Multiple real examples with independent P waves and QRS rhythms. [Open source](https://litfl.com/av-block-3rd-degree-complete-heart-block/)

**ECG gallery: hyperkalaemia (LITFL)** — Illustrates variable severity and non-classical ECG toxicity patterns. [Open source](https://litfl.com/hyperkalaemia-ecg-library/)

**ECG gallery: anterior MI (LITFL)** — Real ECG evolution and reciprocal change. [Open source](https://litfl.com/anterior-myocardial-infarction-ecg-library/)

**ECG gallery: LITFL Top 150** — Self-testing with genuine cases and explanations. [Open source](https://litfl.com/top-100/ecg/)

Figure note: all ECG tracings and explanatory graphics in this handout are newly generated schematic teaching illustrations, not recordings from patients and not validation-quality diagnostic ECGs. Use the linked LITFL examples and clinical 12-lead ECGs to learn true morphology. Clinical decisions must follow actual patient physiology, current protocols and expert assessment.
